y4-2: This is an observational study: it does not prove that ultra-processed food causes fat to build up in muscle, and the dietary information comes from a one-year questionnaire. Fat within the muscle may weaken the muscles that support the knee and so raise the risk of osteoarthritis. When losing weight, it is wise to pay attention not only to calories but also to the quality of what you eat.
y4-3: Researchers examined thigh MRI scans of 615 people from the US Osteoarthritis Initiative who did not yet have knee osteoarthritis but were at risk of it (average age 60). On average, 41% of what participants ate was ultra-processed food. The more ultra-processed food people ate, the more fat had built up within their muscle tissue; this link held regardless of total calorie and fat intake, physical activity and socioeconomic factors.

y4-7: The results come from cell and animal experiments; the drug has not yet been tested in people with osteoarthritis. The effective dose range is narrow: the benefit disappeared at doses that were too high or too low. Because the drug is already approved, clinical trials could move faster. Until then, exercise remains the foundation of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
y4-8: Researchers at Yale School of Medicine showed that a sodium channel called Nav1.7, which is overactive in osteoarthritic joints, both amplifies pain signals and pushes cartilage cells towards breaking down. Lacosamide, which blocks this channel and is already used for epilepsy, supported cartilage building and reduced breakdown at a low dose, and eased joint pain in animals. When the drug was given into the knee inside a collagen gel that sets at body temperature, it stayed in the joint for weeks; a monthly injection prevented cartilage loss better than the drug taken by mouth every day.

y4-12: So far, the drug’s effect has been shown only in animals. Ignaseclant, which works in the same way, has been tested in people with an inherited nerve disease (Charcot-Marie-Tooth), but not yet for muscle weakness in older adults. Today, the most effective treatment for sarcopenia is exercise that works the muscles against resistance.
y4-13: The nerve’s “contract” signal passes to the muscle at a connection point called the neuromuscular junction. In a study led by the University of Missouri, this transmission was found to falter in weak older adults, and the more it faltered, the weaker they were. Older rodents showed the same failure, and a sodium channel called NaV1.4 was reduced in the muscle membrane at the junction. A drug that partly blocks a chloride channel called ClC-1 improved the muscle’s response to nerve signals and muscle function in older rodents.

y4-17: This is an observational study: it does not show that sleep causes these diseases, and diseases not yet diagnosed may already have disturbed sleep. Movement measured at the wrist can only roughly estimate sleep stages. Even so, it is strong evidence of how much regular, sufficient sleep matters.
y4-18: About 96,000 people taking part in the UK Biobank study wore a movement sensor on their wrist for a week, and an artificial intelligence algorithm estimated their sleep stages from the data. Over about 9 years of follow-up, people with more REM sleep at night had a lower risk of 83 diseases: a difference of about 48 minutes of REM sleep was linked to a 26% lower risk of heart failure and a 46% lower risk of dementia. More deep sleep was linked to a lower risk of 7 diseases (including type 2 diabetes and major depression), while irregular sleep and waking during the night were linked to a higher risk of problems such as anxiety. Sleeping less than 5 hours a night was linked to 37 diseases; for most diseases, risk was lowest at 6–8 hours.
